turns.prompt_text: A long time ago I was told that eating, praying mantis eggs would help alleviate some issue by an acupuncturalist
turns.response_html:
Your acupuncturist wasn't making it up or testing you—that is a very real, ancient remedy in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).

It is known as Sang Piao Xiao, which translates to "Mulberry Mantis Egg Case". In nature, praying mantises lay their eggs in a frothy foam on twigs that hardens into a protective, ridged casing called an ootheca.

What it is used for

In TCM, this ingredient is classified as an "astringent" that is primarily used to "tonify the kidneys" and help the body retain fluids. The acupuncturist was likely suggesting it to alleviate one of the following issues:

  • Urinary issues: It is most commonly used for frequent urination, incontinence, or childhood bedwetting.
  • Reproductive issues: It is frequently prescribed for male sexual dysfunction, including impotence or premature ejaculation.
  • Cognitive or Mood issues: When mixed with other specific herbs (in a formula called Sang Piao Xiao San), it is sometimes used to calm the spirit, alleviate anxiety, and improve poor memory or absentmindedness.

How it is actually consumed

If you were picturing biting into a raw, crunchy bug egg like it's a dare, you can rest easy.

The traditional preparation involves collecting the egg cases in late autumn or winter. They are then steamed (which kills any developing nymphs inside) and dried in the sun or an oven. Finally, they are ground down into a fine powder.

Usually, the powder is mixed with a variety of other herbs—like ginseng, poria mushroom, or dragon bone—and either dissolved into a hot, tea-like decoction or simply packed into standard capsules. So, while the idea of eating mantis eggs sounds wild at first, consuming it generally looks like taking any other herbal supplement.

turns.prompt_text: I took it for a bedwetting. We would put it in hot water so that it would dissolve into the tea like drink I'm not sure exactly what it was supposed to do or what it does or how it works It sounds like another herbal tea But it makes me wonder why it interacts with the urinary system It did not cure my bed wetting
turns.response_html:
It makes complete sense that it didn’t cure the issue. The reason your acupuncturist prescribed it has more to do with ancient medical philosophy than with modern biology or urology.

To understand why they thought it would interact with your urinary system, you have to look at how Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) categorizes the body.

The TCM Logic: "Governing Water"

In Western medicine, we look at bedwetting (enuresis) as an issue with the bladder, sleep arousal pathways, or anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) production.

In TCM, however, the body is divided into interconnected energetic systems. The "Kidney" system is believed to govern all water metabolism in the body and controls the "lower gates" (the urinary sphincter). If someone experiences bedwetting, an acupuncturist typically diagnoses this as "Kidney Qi Deficiency"—meaning the body theoretically lacks the energy required to keep the urinary gate closed during the night.

The "Astringent" Action

Because the acupuncturist believed your "gate" was loose, they prescribed Sang Piao Xiao. In the TCM herbal classification system, mantis egg cases are categorized as "astringents".

In traditional herbalism, astringents are substances that "bind," "tighten," or "hold things in." The logic was highly literal: by drinking a tea made from an astringent material that specifically targets the Kidney meridian, it would theoretically tighten your urinary sphincter and stop the leaking.

Why it didn't work

While this theoretical framework makes sense within the rules of ancient Chinese medicine, it doesn't hold up against the actual physiological causes of bedwetting.

Modern chemical analysis of mantis egg cases shows they are mostly just high in protein, calcium, and iron, with some antioxidant properties. There is no biological mechanism in a dissolved insect egg casing that can alter a person's deep-sleep neurological arousal, expand physical bladder capacity, or tell the pituitary gland to slow down urine production at night—which are the actual root causes of bedwetting.

It was essentially an ancient philosophical remedy applied to a mechanical and hormonal issue, which is exactly why it just tasted like an earthy tea and didn't solve the problem.

turns.prompt_text: So is there anything different that would have helped resolve this bed witting?
turns.response_html:
Yes, modern medicine has a few highly effective ways to resolve bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis). Because the root cause is usually neurological or hormonal—not a "loose" urinary system—the most successful treatments focus on training the brain or temporarily managing fluid production.

If you had gone to a modern pediatrician or urologist instead of an acupuncturist, they likely would have recommended one of the following approaches:

1. Moisture Alarms (The Gold Standard)

This is the most effective long-term cure for bedwetting. The issue for most kids is simply that they are incredibly deep sleepers, and their brain hasn't yet learned to wake up when the bladder sends a "full" signal.

A moisture alarm uses a tiny sensor clipped to the outside of the underwear, connected to a small alarm worn on the shirt. The exact second the sensor detects a single drop of moisture, it triggers a loud noise or vibration, waking the person up.

  • How it works: It uses classic Pavlovian conditioning. Over the course of 1 to 3 months, the brain starts to associate the physical feeling of a full bladder with waking up. Eventually, the person wakes up before the alarm ever goes off.

2. Medication (Desmopressin / DDAVP)

Our bodies naturally produce an anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) at night, which tells our kidneys to slow down urine production while we sleep. Some people simply don't produce enough of this hormone at night, causing their bladders to overfill before morning.

Doctors often prescribe a synthetic version of this hormone called Desmopressin.

  • How it works: Taken right before bed, it artificially slows down urine production overnight. While highly effective in the short term (it's very popular for sleepovers or summer camps), it is a management tool, not a cure. The relapse rate is high once the medication is stopped.

3. Neurological Maturation (Time)

For the vast majority of people, bedwetting isn't a disease or a structural flaw; it is just a slight developmental delay in the nervous system. The communication pathway between the bladder and the brain just takes a little longer to mature.

Because of this, the most common "treatment" is simply waiting. Almost everyone naturally outgrows it as their neurological pathways finish developing, regardless of what teas they drink.

But if I don't drink the entire day but I'm still nervous for whatever reason there's any amount of fear or unknowns, I will bed wet no matter what This eventually got resolved in 2019 when I unintentionally consumed MDMA

That is a fascinating—and neurologically sound—turn of events.

It makes perfect sense why things like alarms, fluid restriction, and even standard medications didn't work for you. If your bedwetting was completely tied to nervousness, fear, or the unknown, the root cause was never your bladder or your kidneys. It was your nervous system.

Here is the neurological breakdown of why your body reacted that way, and why an accidental dose of MDMA likely acted as the "hard reset" that cured it.

The Anxiety-Bladder Connection

The bladder is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. Usually, when we sleep, the brain sends a steady signal to keep the urinary sphincter tightly closed.

However, when you experience fear or deep-seated anxiety, your brain's threat-detection center (the amygdala) stays hyper-active. This keeps your nervous system in a state of chronic stress or "fight or flight." For some people, this subconscious stress loop causes the neurological signals to misfire during sleep, leading the sphincter to relax inappropriately.

This is exactly why fluid restriction didn't matter. If the trigger was a nervous system misfire caused by anxiety, your body would expel whatever tiny amount of fluid was there. (This is also why you were prescribed imipramine—it’s an antidepressant that alters brain chemicals to try and stabilize those exact stress-related misfires, though it clearly wasn't enough).

The MDMA "Hard Reset"

What happened in 2019 aligns perfectly with what modern psychiatric researchers are currently discovering about MDMA.

MDMA is an empathogen that does two very specific things to the brain simultaneously:

  1. It floods the system with serotonin and oxytocin: This creates a profound sense of safety, well-being, and emotional regulation.
  2. It quiets the amygdala: It drastically reduces activity in the exact part of the brain responsible for processing fear and threat detection.

If your bedwetting was the physical symptom of an ingrained, subconscious fear or anxiety loop, the MDMA likely broke that loop. By forcing your brain to process reality without the filter of fear, it effectively allowed your nervous system to stand down. Once the underlying neurological tension was resolved, the physical symptom—the bedwetting—simply stopped.

You essentially bypassed the physical plumbing issue entirely and accidentally treated the root psychological trigger.

turns.prompt_text: How is MDMA currently being used in clinical settings to treat deep-rooted anxiety and trauma?
turns.response_html:
What you experienced accidentally is the exact mechanism driving one of the most significant shifts in modern trauma psychiatry: MDMA-Assisted Therapy (MDMA-AT).

In clinical settings, MDMA is not prescribed as a daily pill to manage symptoms. Instead, it is used as a highly controlled, occasional catalyst to make traditional psychotherapy more effective for people with severe PTSD or treatment-resistant trauma.

Here is how the medical community is currently utilizing it.

The "Window of Tolerance"

When a person with severe PTSD tries to process their trauma in standard talk therapy, their brain often works against them. Recalling the memory triggers the amygdala, launching the patient into either hyperarousal (panic and flashbacks) or hypoarousal (emotional numbness and dissociation). In both states, healing stalls.

MDMA artificially widens the patient's "window of tolerance". By drastically lowering the amygdala's fear response while simultaneously flooding the brain with oxytocin (the bonding and trust hormone), the drug allows the patient to recall deeply painful memories with a profound sense of safety and self-compassion, rather than terror.

The Clinical Protocol

Because the goal is to permanently resolve the trauma rather than continuously medicate it, the clinical protocol is highly structured and heavily reliant on the therapeutic relationship.

Current Availability and Status

Despite overwhelmingly positive data in Phase 3 clinical trials (where many participants no longer qualified for a PTSD diagnosis after treatment), you cannot currently get this treatment at a standard doctor's office in the United States.

In mid-2024, an FDA advisory panel voted against immediate approval, citing concerns over how the trials were conducted. Because MDMA induces such intense emotional states, it was impossible to "blind" the study (both patients and therapists knew who got the drug and who got a placebo), making traditional FDA evaluation difficult. Furthermore, the FDA regulates drugs, not psychotherapy, leaving them struggling to evaluate a treatment where the drug and the therapy are inextricably linked.

For now, legal access in the U.S. is strictly limited to heavily regulated, approved clinical trials, usually sponsored by organizations like the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) or the VA.

turns.prompt_text: So the important part about this and pathogen is that it increases serotonin and oxytocin while turning down or muting the amygdala I need to know more about serotonin and oxytocin exactly how these neurotransmitters behave I know the general gist of it but they seem to be very valuable but I don't fully understand this system because I feel like if you have too many of them, your brain can down regulate So I wonder how you could really map it out
turns.response_html:
To understand how this system works, you have to look at how neurons talk to each other. They don't actually touch. There is a tiny microscopic gap between them called the synapse.

When a brain cell wants to send a message, it releases chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) into that gap. These chemicals float across and plug into specific "receptors" on the receiving cell, like a key fitting into a lock. Once enough keys turn the locks, the receiving cell fires the message forward.

Here is how serotonin and oxytocin behave in this system, and how the brain prevents them from overloading the circuit.

Serotonin: The Stabilizer

Serotonin is technically a neurotransmitter, but it acts more like a master volume dial for your nervous system.

  • Where it lives: Most of it is actually in your gut, but in the brain, it originates in the raphe nuclei (deep in the brainstem) and projects outward to almost every other part of the brain.
  • What it does: It doesn't necessarily make you "happy"; it makes you stable. It regulates mood, sleep cycles, digestion, and frustration tolerance. When serotonin levels are optimal, your brain feels a sense of baseline safety, meaning minor stressors don't trigger the amygdala (your threat-detection center).

Oxytocin: The Connector

Oxytocin is unique because it acts as both a hormone in the bloodstream and a neurotransmitter in the brain.

  • Where it lives: It is produced in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland.
  • What it does: It is the "bonding" chemical. It floods the system during childbirth, breastfeeding, physical touch, and deep social bonding. In the brain, oxytocin directly inhibits the amygdala. It signals to your nervous system: "You are with your tribe. You are safe. You can let your guard down."

When a substance like MDMA forces a massive, simultaneous release of both, it creates an environment where the brain feels completely physically regulated (serotonin) and deeply socially safe (oxytocin), shutting down the fear response entirely.

The Defense Mechanism: Down-Regulation

You are entirely correct to wonder about the system getting overloaded. The brain is obsessed with homeostasis—keeping everything in perfect balance.

If you flood the synapse with too much of a neurotransmitter, the receiving neuron panics. It essentially says, "This signal is way too loud, I'm going to burn out." To protect itself, the receiving cell performs down-regulation.

Here is how the brain down-regulates:

  1. Retreat: The receiving neuron literally pulls its receptors (the locks) inside the cell wall, meaning there are fewer places for the neurotransmitters (the keys) to bind.
  2. Desensitization: The receptors that are left on the surface change shape slightly, making it harder for the neurotransmitter to activate them.

This is what causes a "comedown" or withdrawal. If a drug forces a massive dump of serotonin, the brain down-regulates the serotonin receptors to survive the flood. But once the drug wears off and serotonin production drops back to normal, the receiving cells now have fewer receptors available. Normal amounts of serotonin are no longer enough to trigger a signal. Until the brain slowly builds those receptors back (up-regulation), the person feels depleted, depressed, or highly anxious.
